newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Hollywood writers lament sorry state of film.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Hollywood writers lament sorry state of film.

text.p: Many Hollywood writers have lost the thrill of the chase scene, but they have few choices in a studio system that loves fast action and special effects.

"Sometimes I want to thumb my nose at the system, but I always wind up liking what I'm writing," said Katherine Reback, who is writing the screenplay for "I Dream of Jeannie," a film based on the popular television series.

Reback, who wrote speeches for President Bill Clinton in 1991 and 1992, joined other screenwriters at a recent Writers Guild forum where many complained about the lack of character and plot development in films now dominating the box office.
While writers scoff at the big-action genre, industry insiders admit such films are hard to turn down, expecially when studios pay writers as much as $4 million a script.

Among the highest paid are Shane Black, who penned "The Long Kiss Goodnight," and Joe Eszterhas, who wrote "Jade" and "Basic Instinct." The Writers Guild minimum rate is $28,537 for a low-budget movie costing less than $2.5 million and $58,411 for movies that cost above that amount.
Agents, who help writers secure contracts, bear some responsibility for the state of affairs, according to Jeremy Zimmer, a partner of the United Talent Agency.
AGENTS FEAR LOSING CLIENTS

"Due to the competitive nature of the business, agents are afraid of losing a client (writer) and telling clients the truth about projects. That's why we're getting such lousy movies," Zimmer said during a panel at the forum. "The seductive money available is making it hard to say no and the quality in studio movies has diminished because of the intense merchandising aspects."
Hollywood has already begun to roll out a summer slate of special effect extravaganzas such as "The Lost World:Jurassic Park" hoping to rake in billions of dollars in ticket sales.

Last year, the film business scored a record $2.4 billion in summer box office sales, 40 percent of the year's total take, with the help of high-adventure thrillers such as "Independence Day," "Twister" and "Mission:Impossible."

"Most movies should never have been made because most movies are evil and horrible," said Wallace Shawn, whose writing credits include the critically acclaimed "My Dinner with Andre," in which he also starred.

"Most movies promote the status quo, which I think should be changed and not accepted. They even go further by propagating particularly horrible tendencies like lust for revenge, nauseating stereotypes, militarism, the belief that macho attitudes will solve our problems," Shawn said.

Violence is discussed but not shown in Shawn's just-opened film, "The Designated Mourner," starring Mike Nichols. But Shawn quickly notes that his films are not commercial giants. "It's a very tiny film," he said.
MIDDLE-BUDGET FILMS BECOMING EXTINCT

Indeed, many writers said there is very little middle ground between huge blockbuster costing more than $100 million and low-budget independent films. Modest, middle-budget films costing $15 million to $40 million are becoming extinct.

Seasoned writers said it may be easier to break into the business with a $100 million movie or a low-budget art film than through a mid-sized movie with a good storyline, which was the conventional wisdom a few years ago.

"I consider the time I broke in was when I optioned a police thriller and everybody was writing police thrillers," said Billy Bob Thornton, who won an Academy Award this year for best screenplay adaption for "Sling Blade," a provocative independent film he starred in and directed.
"There's a real difference between breaking in and doing stuff from your heart," Thornton said.
Meanwhile, opportunities for scriptwriters are shrinking on the small screen as NBC and CBS both recently opted to drop one of their two movie-of-the week slots this September.

"TV movies are marginally more expensive to make than episodes for a series," said Tom Cook, a Writers Guild board member. "This is an economic move by the networks and it will cost a lot of writers work and tension. At the same time, it may improve the quality of TV films."

Networks in the past few years have seen ratings fall for television movies and some writers said this was partly due to a preponderance of projects with the "women in peril" theme starring popular actresses from television shows like "Melrose Place" and "Beverly Hills, 90210."
